The taxi driver offered to carry Naomi's case upstairs, but she paid him at the kerb and said the handle was stronger than it looked. It was something her mother might have said. The case had a cracked wheel and a strip of bright airline tape that seemed indecent against the bakery's pale brickwork. Across the window, someone had painted BELL & FAMILY in letters too small to conceal the old outline of BELL & SON. Naomi had helped her father scrape that window when she was seventeen. Now a stack of folded delivery trays stood where he used to keep the stool, and the bell over the door made an unfamiliar, economical click.

Naomi set the brass key in Ruth’s palm. Ruth closed her hand around it and said the lock caught only when someone pulled before turning. Naomi knew Ruth now held the brass key. Naomi trusted Daniel to carry the shopping, but no longer trusted his account of the family papers. That knowledge had none of the comfort of possession. She would have to knock if she went out late. Ruth would know whether she returned. The small mechanics of living together were already organising a conversation they had not yet agreed to have.

[noncontiguous passage]

It was dented at one corner and had once held biscuits Naomi was forbidden to eat before Christmas. Ruth opened it with her body between the lid and the stairs. Naomi saw paper edges, not their contents. She wanted to say she was not a child who needed shielding from a bill. Instead she asked whether there was enough tea. Ruth said there was always enough tea if people remembered where it was kept. The remark carried no obvious injury, but Naomi heard in it every year she had been away.

[noncontiguous passage]

She unpacked only what she needed for the night. The upstairs room smelled of dry wood and warm yeast rising through the floor. She placed the plaster wrapper in the bin rather than leaving it on the bedside table, a small effort to make her presence seem manageable. Below her, Ruth turned the oven dial and Daniel drew the back bolt. The sound of each action reached her clearly. Naomi stayed in the upstairs apartment after the bakery closed. She listened until the house had finished its evening arrangements and then lay down without opening her laptop. For the first time in months there was no meeting to prepare for, and she found the absence more alarming than the work. Ruth believed her children would stay for supper.

The bakery had always made its earliest sound before it made its first light. Naomi heard the mixer settling through the floor and knew that Daniel had started it while the street was still dark. She dressed slowly, feeling the pull of the healing cut when she buttoned her sleeve. The apartment looked less like a room waiting for a guest to leave. Her case stood open, her notebook lay beside the bed, and the chair she had avoided moving now held a clean stack of towels. Naomi opened the bakery before dawn. Cold air entered with her, carrying the distant rush of a street-cleaning vehicle and the ordinary prospect of work.

[noncontiguous passage]

“I thought a locked door would keep you both safe,” Ruth said. She was watching the key beside the till, not either of their faces. Daniel asked safe from what. Ruth named debts, arguments, the difficulty of telling children that a parent had changed their mind too late to say so in person. These were explanations of her choices, not proof that every choice had been necessary. Naomi told her that she had felt protected from the facts rather than protected by them. Ruth did not answer immediately. The shop required attention; a customer wanted yesterday's order checked, and for several minutes all three took refuge in counting out what was actually owed.

[noncontiguous passage]

Naomi entrusted the letter to Mrs. Ames for the family archive. They agreed that anyone in the family could read it, and that a copy would remain in the bakery. Mrs. Ames wrote those conditions on the folder before accepting it. The small ceremony pleased Naomi more than she expected. It made safekeeping a task with stated limits, rather than another person's permission to decide when information might be useful. Daniel placed the unsigned receipt beside the letter, then changed his mind and kept a copy. They were learning, clumsily, to distinguish a shared history from a single object that one person had to guard.

[noncontiguous passage]

That evening, Ruth ate at the table while someone else checked the oven. Daniel described a faulty pedal at the hall, and Naomi told him about the customer who preferred the darker loaf. Their conversation did not return to the letter until they were nearly finished. Then Ruth said that she wished their father had delivered it himself. Neither child tried to make that wish reasonable. They allowed it to sit beside what had actually happened, without confusing the two. Outside, the window reflected the new word FAMILY across the cleared counter. Naomi noticed that the old outline beneath it was still visible and found that she no longer wanted the painter to cover it more thoroughly. Daniel believed their mother would enjoy hearing the piano in the hall.

The newspaper boy brought the threat folded inside an advertisement for winter coal. Elise found this almost considerate: the shop was cold, and an honest offer of fuel would have been more useful than another demand that Miriam surrender her licence. She spread the papers beneath the window, where the late light caught every uneven letter. The disputed leaflet accused the printer of issuing a notice under a name she had no right to use. It bore no signature of its own. The disputed leaflet carried a watermark shaped like a broken wheel. Elise held it above the clean sheet used to protect the composing stone. The wheel was pale and incomplete, as if somebody had lifted the paper before the mark was finished. A watermark could place a sheet in a history, though it could not tell her who had written the words upon it.

[noncontiguous passage]

Pike arrived while she was warming a line of type beside the small stove. “The council has cancelled your licence,” Pike said. He did not show a council order. He said the official copy would follow and looked at the cold press as if it had already become somebody else's property. Elise asked which date the cancellation carried. The constable told her not to be clever. She had spent years being praised for clever fingers and punished for clever questions, and she kept her hand too close to the metal while deciding which reply would cost Miriam least. The hot type burned Elise’s right thumb. The pain was immediate and usefully simple. She put her thumb under the cold tap, asked again for the date, and watched Pike turn his attention to a crack in the floor. Miriam offered him a chair. He declined it as though sitting down might count as negotiation.

[noncontiguous passage]

Elise stayed beside the stone after Jonas went upstairs to fetch his coat. Elise remembered the attic room she had rented during her first apprenticeship. She had slept there above the cooper's hammering and carried her washing to a pump that froze every second winter. She could no longer put a year to the beginning of that apprenticeship. She remembered only the effort of learning to distinguish similar letters by touch when the candle failed. Tonight the same habit made her notice the wrong letter before she noticed the meaning of the sentence around it. It was a small competence and an inadequate defence against a constable, but it was hers. Elise could not decide whether the cart outside belonged to the constable. A cart stood beyond the window, its driver turned away under a broad hat. She could hear no conversation and would not claim that the shop was being watched merely because she was frightened enough to watch it herself.

[noncontiguous passage]

Miriam sent Jonas to ask the neighbours for a dry place to store the unspoiled stock. Elise watched him cross the yard, then looked towards the bridge. Pike took his post at the stone toll bridge. Pike's coat made a dark patch beside the toll board. He had ordinary duties as well as the power to make an unsupported statement in their doorway, a fact she found harder to accommodate than an image of him as nothing but an enemy. She wrapped the burnt thumb, copied the licence date into her notebook, and prepared the samples for the morning. The printer's name at the foot of the disputed leaflet was wrong in a way that now seemed deliberate. She did not yet know whose purpose it served, and she resisted granting the mystery a single author before she had traced its paper.

She looked at her equipment as if it belonged to another engineer: the notebooks swollen by taped photographs, the wafer clasp polished by repeated checks, a screwdriver marked with Anton's initials. She put the screwdriver in the sealed effects bag and kept the notebooks inside her suit. Nia crossed into the rescue shuttle carrying the final log. The shuttle smelled of fabric warmed too quickly and a meal she could not identify. Its ordinary clutter was more unsettling than a sterile emergency cabin would have been. Someone had drawn a small bird on the back of a restraint seat. She touched the drawing with one gloved finger while the pilot waited for her to acknowledge the transfer list.

[noncontiguous passage]

The inspection drone came through last, folded and dark, its camera lens turned towards the floor. The rescue service accepted the inspection drone into its equipment register. Nia signed beside the equipment number and added that its stored images belonged with the audit. The last patch roll remained sealed inside the abandoned habitat. She had wanted to bring that roll, absurdly, because leaving a repair material felt like deciding that no one would return. The pilot had allowed only the log and the items already sealed. A future salvage crew could retrieve the rest if the habitat remained intact. That conditional sentence was harder to hear than a firm order. Nia wrote the roll's location on the abandonment sheet, resisting the impulse to change remained into lost. A thing could still exist somewhere she was no longer able to reach it.

[noncontiguous passage]

Nia read the temporary appointment twice. It gave her a duty, not a promotion she could celebrate. Mira said the inquiry would ask why they had taken a failed test cell on the inventory instead of discarding it. Nia answered that the cell explained a number. They rehearsed no other answers. A rehearsed account might become smoother than the events, and smoothness was precisely what the old graph had offered on both sides of its silence. She intended to testify at the inquiry after reaching the relay. For now she recorded what she had touched, what she had heard, what another person had reported, and what she had merely inferred. The page was untidy enough to be useful.

The relay appeared first as an extra point on the navigation display. The pilot sent their receipt code and waited for a channel assignment. Nia could only guess whether another habitat would answer before their orbit changed. Another habitat might answer later, or might never receive the call. She left those possibilities outside the casualty list. Europa had dwindled to a bright, damaged-looking coin beyond the shuttle's tail, though no coin could have held so much cold. Mira asked whether Nia wanted the empty seat cleared of its equipment straps. Nia said to leave them until the transfer was complete. It was a request about a seat, and she was grateful that Mira accepted it on that scale. They watched the reader make its second copy while the relay grew brighter and the cabin began to smell faintly of someone else's coffee.
